doc.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Standing ovations at the Annie Ross reunion at the Blue Note
summary: The reunion with Annie Ross drew 12-15 minute ovations and three generations of fans.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: Well gosh I know a lot has happened to you since the last time we spoke. You just finished an engagement with Annie Ross?

Yeah, that’s a phenomenon I’m very happy I lived to see because being in show business, since seven, there are things that you see that you expect to see. You expect it if you do well in your act, people will give you applause and they’ll love you and they’ll want you to come back. This you expect. But I never saw what happened when Annie Ross and I got back together. And that is, the minute we were introduced and walked on stage, the whole house stood up and applauded for 12-15 minutes. And I never saw this in my whole life. This was quite something. And I still am at a loss to say what it is, really. Because I don’t want to overpraise what is happening but I don’t want to underpraise it either. I think it’s a validation of the fact that in creating words for big band arrangements — which is what Leonard Feather dubbed “vocalese” — I stumbled upon a new cultural art form. And this attitude of these people who stand up when we walk on is validation of that. It gives it its bona fides you know. I did something.

It sure did, and it lasted. I mean that music has been out there for some 40 years now, and hit on different generations, and I think people responded to the quality and the longevity of it, and thus that kind of ovation.

Yeah. And I was also heartened and kind of amazed, because it both exhilarated Annie and me, but brought to my attention something that I try not to pay too much attention to which is age — the fact that I was entertaining three generations. People came with their © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -5-

grown sons and daughters and their children’s records. They all had the albums. See it was three generations looking at us: grandpa and grandma, who were the big hard core fans forty years ago; their sons, 24, 25, out of college you know with their wives; and their kids, with the albums. And I said how old does that make me? It’s amazing. It really takes your breath away. It starts you to thinking, good Lord, that’s quite something. I think that’s really interesting. Well you know Duke did that too. He told me about that — where he’d meet these kids at these proms and they would say, “my grandfather said he first heard you — .” And Duke would say “oh that was my son.”
